Adult Sepsis: Recognition and Early Management (Sample)

Recognition.
Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host
response to infection. Suspect sepsis in any patient with a known or likely
infection who shows signs of clinical deterioration. High-risk criteria include
a respiratory rate of 25 breaths per minute or more, oxygen saturation below 92
percent, heart rate above 130 beats per minute, systolic blood pressure of 90
mmHg or lower, new altered mental state, and no urine output for the previous 18
hours. The presence of any single high-risk criterion warrants immediate senior
clinical review.

Initial assessment.
Measure a full set of vital signs including temperature, heart rate, respiratory
rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation and level of consciousness. Measure
serum lactate and obtain blood cultures before starting antibiotics where this
does not delay treatment. Venous or arterial lactate above 2 mmol/L indicates
tissue hypoperfusion, and a level above 4 mmol/L indicates high risk and the
need for urgent resuscitation.

The Sepsis Six.
For patients with suspected sepsis and high-risk features, deliver the following
six interventions within one hour of recognition: administer high-flow oxygen to
maintain target saturations, take blood cultures, give broad-spectrum
intravenous antibiotics, give intravenous fluids, measure serum lactate, and
monitor urine output. This bundle is intended to be completed within the first
hour, sometimes called the golden hour.

Antibiotics.
Give broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics in line with local microbiology
policy within one hour of identifying high-risk sepsis. Do not wait for blood
culture results before starting treatment. Review the choice of antibiotic once
culture sensitivities are available and de-escalate where appropriate to reduce
the risk of antimicrobial resistance.

Fluid resuscitation.
For adults with suspected sepsis and a lactate above 2 mmol/L or hypotension,
give an intravenous crystalloid fluid bolus of 500 mL over less than 15 minutes
and reassess. Repeated boluses may be required, with careful monitoring for
signs of fluid overload, particularly in older adults and those with heart
failure or chronic kidney disease.

Escalation.
Escalate to critical care for patients who remain hypotensive or have a
persistently raised lactate despite initial fluid resuscitation, as these
patients may require vasopressor support. Senior clinical decision making should
not be delayed.

Children.
The thresholds and physiological values described above apply to adults. Paediatric
sepsis uses age-specific vital sign thresholds and is outside the scope of this
sample document.
